# Days Until Warmer — Explained, One Approach at a Time

     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Stack** · medium · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/daily-temperatures/)

Given daily temperatures, return an array where answer[i] is the number of days you wait after day i for a strictly warmer temperature, or 0 if it never comes.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= temperatures.length <= 10^5
- 30 <= temperatures[i] <= 100
- a day with no warmer day ahead answers 0

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `temps = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]` | `[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]` | — |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Brute force re-scans the future for every day. Notice which days are still "waiting".
2. Keep waiting days on a stack. A new temperature resolves every colder day on top of it.
3. The stack stays in decreasing temperature order — that invariant is the whole trick (monotonic stack).

</details>

---

## 1. Brute force

For each day, scan forward until something warmer shows up.

```python
def daily_warmer(temps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(temps)
    answer = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if temps[j] > temps[i]:
                answer[i] = j - i
                break
    return answer
```

**O(n²) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] dailyWarmer(int[] temps) {
    int n = temps.length;
    int[] answer = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (temps[j] > temps[i]) {
                answer[i] = j - i;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    return answer;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> dailyWarmer(const vector<int>& temps) {
    int n = (int)temps.size();
    vector<int> answer(n, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (temps[j] > temps[i]) {
                answer[i] = j - i;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    return answer;
}
```

## 2. Backward scan

> **Why now.** Scanning forward from every day re-walks the same runs of cold days. Going right to left lets each day hop over stretches that already have answers.

Iterate right-to-left; from day i, hop through already-computed answers to skip runs of colder days. Same worst case on paper, but each hop jumps a whole resolved block — a nice trick when a stack feels heavyweight.

```python
def daily_warmer(temps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(temps)
    answer = [0] * n
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        j = i + 1
        while j < n and temps[j] <= temps[i]:
            if answer[j] == 0:
                j = n  # nothing warmer ever again
            else:
                j += answer[j]
        answer[i] = j - i if j < n else 0
    return answer
```

**O(n) amortized time · O(1) extra space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] dailyWarmer(int[] temps) {
    int n = temps.length;
    int[] answer = new int[n];
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
        int j = i + 1;
        while (j < n && temps[j] <= temps[i]) {
            if (answer[j] == 0) {
                j = n;
            } else {
                j += answer[j];
            }
        }
        answer[i] = (j < n) ? (j - i) : 0;
    }
    return answer;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> dailyWarmer(const vector<int>& temps) {
    int n = (int)temps.size();
    vector<int> answer(n, 0);
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; --i) {
        int j = i + 1;
        while (j < n && temps[j] <= temps[i]) {
            if (answer[j] == 0) {
                j = n;
            } else {
                j += answer[j];
            }
        }
        answer[i] = (j < n) ? (j - i) : 0;
    }
    return answer;
}
```

</details>

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Those hops still depend on the shape of the data. A stack of days still waiting for something warmer gives every day exactly one push and one pop, whatever the input looks like.

Hold a stack of indices whose warmer day hasn't arrived, always in decreasing temperature order. Each new day pops every index with a colder temperature — the gap in indices is that day's answer — then pushes itself. Every index is pushed and popped at most once, so the pass is linear.

```python
def daily_warmer(temps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    answer = [0] * len(temps)
    waiting: list[int] = []  # indices, temps decreasing
    for i, t in enumerate(temps):
        while waiting and temps[waiting[-1]] < t:
            j = waiting.pop()
            answer[j] = i - j
        waiting.append(i)
    return answer
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] dailyWarmer(int[] temps) {
    int n = temps.length;
    int[] answer = new int[n];
    int[] stack = new int[n];
    int sp = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (sp > 0 && temps[stack[sp - 1]] < temps[i]) {
            int j = stack[--sp];
            answer[j] = i - j;
        }
        stack[sp++] = i;
    }
    return answer;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> dailyWarmer(const vector<int>& temps) {
    int n = (int)temps.size();
    vector<int> answer(n);
    vector<int> stack; stack.reserve(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (!stack.empty() && temps[stack.back()] < temps[i]) {
            int j = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
            answer[j] = i - j;
        }
        stack.push_back(i);
    }
    return answer;
}
```

</details>

---

## The arc

The monotonic stack, learned once and reused forever. The stack holds indices whose answer is still unknown, kept in decreasing temperature order, and the moment a warmer day arrives it resolves every index it beats — each index enters and leaves exactly once, which is why an inner while loop is still linear overall. The backward rung is the same information travelling the other way, and comparing the two is the best way to see that this is 'next greater element' in disguise. Learn to recognise the family: next greater, next smaller, previous greater, span problems, and largest rectangle are one technique with the comparison and the direction changed.

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brute force | O(n²) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Backward scan | O(n) amortized time · O(1) extra space | Scanning forward from every day re-walks the same runs of cold days. Going right to left lets each day hop over stretches that already have answers. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(n) space | Those hops still depend on the shape of the data. A stack of days still waiting for something warmer gives every day exactly one push and one pop, whatever the input looks like. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def daily_warmer_brute_force(temps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(temps)
    answer = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if temps[j] > temps[i]:
                answer[i] = j - i
                break
    return answer


def daily_warmer_backward_scan(temps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(temps)
    answer = [0] * n
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        j = i + 1
        while j < n and temps[j] <= temps[i]:
            if answer[j] == 0:
                j = n  # nothing warmer ever again
            else:
                j += answer[j]
        answer[i] = j - i if j < n else 0
    return answer


def daily_warmer_the_one_to_remember(temps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    answer = [0] * len(temps)
    waiting: list[int] = []  # indices, temps decreasing
    for i, t in enumerate(temps):
        while waiting and temps[waiting[-1]] < t:
            j = waiting.pop()
            answer[j] = i - j
        waiting.append(i)
    return answer

APPROACHES = [
    daily_warmer_brute_force,
    daily_warmer_backward_scan,
    daily_warmer_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# equal temperatures, which are NOT warmer — [50,40,30,30] answers all zeros
CASES = [
    lambda: ([50,40,30,30],),
    lambda: ([73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73],),
    lambda: ([30,40,50,60],),
    lambda: ([30],),
    lambda: ([50,40,30],),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<34} -> {answers}")
```
